prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision measurement of time

statement.case_for: I keep the single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. My criterion is whether a technique changes what can be measured, and has been shown to do so by independent groups. The magic-wavelength condition cancels the light shift by design, so thousands of atoms are interrogated without Doppler or recoil broadening. The record-accuracy realisation then took that to about 1e-18. The strongest evidence is not one laboratory's number but comparisons between independent clocks at JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, which are the measurement equivalent of replication. The clocks have already produced physics: millimetre-scale gravitational redshift, bounds on variation of constants, dark-matter searches, and many-body effects inside the clock. On the chair's first question, the distinction from 2005 and 2012 can be put in the citation. The comb (2005) is a ruler for optical frequencies. The 2012 prize concerned control of single quantum systems, and the best ion clocks are limited by one ion's signal-to-noise. The lattice clock gets its stability from interrogating many neutral atoms at once with the lattice perturbation cancelled, which is a different route to the precision regime. The citation should name the invention and the realisation, not just 'precision'. After round 1 my view of the scientific case is unchanged, and my confidence has risen because six of eight members converge on it from different subfields.
statement.case_against: The reservations are unchanged but I can now say which are judgement and which are checkable. Whether this is a discovery or an instrument is judgement. My answer is that the committee has honoured measurement inventions that opened new physics, and this one already has. Credit is partly checkable. A report should confirm from the first publications who proposed the magic-wavelength lattice (Katori and collaborators, 2003) and who first demonstrated and then drove strontium lattice clocks to the accuracy frontier. It should also state what Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom contributed separately, since several members (and I) are working from memory. The weaker point is timing. The SI second has not been redefined. I treat that as an argument about timing, not maturity: the scientific demonstration, the multi-laboratory comparisons and the 1e-18 uncertainty budgets exist now, and waiting for a metrological ceremony would make the Nobel prize follow the standards bodies. Two names will leave good people out, and I do not hide that.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks B007 only fifth because it is an invention and a precision-measurement result rather than a new state of matter, and fears a third step in the precision-spectroscopy chain after 2005 and 2012. He also says the two cases are not in conflict.
responses.response: I agree that the two cases are not in conflict, and I take the overlap concern seriously enough to answer it on the physics. The 2005 prize covered the comb and the 2012 prize covered control of single ions and photons. Neither covers neutral atoms held in an engineered lattice with the light shift cancelled, which is what gives the stability. A twenty-year-old technique with independent clock comparisons is also easier for me to defend than a young field with an open mechanism. I do not think a clock needs to be a new state of matter to be a discovery, but I accept that this is where we differ in judgement. His point that B001 opens a field with no earlier prize is strong, and it is why I keep B001 as my first alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers B001 because a simple analytical model made a sharp prediction that was verified. He argues that an unresolved pairing mechanism is not a maturity problem, using cuprates as the example, and says B007 is the more mature and less contested fallback.
responses.response: The cuprate analogy is fair, and I withdraw part of my earlier statement that the open pairing mechanism makes B001 immature. The discovery of correlated and superconducting phases at the magic angle is established. My remaining difference is about attribution and age. Bistritzer-MacDonald is clean, but the experimental side leaves out Cao and the first authors, and device-to-device variation from twist-angle disorder is still a measurement problem. For the lattice clock, the stability and reproducibility have been tested for longer by independent comparisons. I also value that Mehlig names B007 as his fallback. That says the committee is not split on the science, only on which of two good candidates is ready first.

responses.point: Johansson says my interest in matter-wave interferometry (B021) as a close second is weaker than B007 alone, because of credit problems with Chu, Bordé, Pritchard and Kasevich, and that B007 alone is more defensible than a split prize.
responses.response: I accept that. B021 did not reach the shortlist, and a credit dispute among four or five names is exactly what a split prize cannot absorb. I also take his point that a two-part prize here would force dropping a name from B007 to stay within three people, and that would damage the cleanest feature of the configuration. I therefore stay with a single part. Johansson's recusal note on B058 is the right procedure, and it leaves the Chalmers circuit-QED question for a later year.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B007 first, with B001 and B039 as alternatives, and in round 1 raised Lemonde and Ludlow as possible additions to the credit and the redefinition of the second as a measure of maturity.
responses.response: I agree with the ranking and with his view of the redefinition as evidence of community acceptance. In round 1 I said the ion-clock community was largely covered in 2012. I now think I stated it too firmly. The ion clocks are covered as a technology, but the lattice-clock credit is a separate question that needs the record, not my memory. The three-name limit permits a third name. I would add one only if the report shows an identifiable, separable step by Lemonde, Ludlow or Hinkley that is as fundamental as the magic-wavelength proposal or the accuracy realisation, and I do not expect it to. If the report does show one, the two-name citation must change.

responses.point: The chair asks whether the committee can state why B007 is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, and whether a prize should precede or follow the redefinition of the second, and whether this is an argument about maturity or only about timing.
responses.response: As a distinction I would write it into the citation: the invention of a neutral-atom clock in which a magic-wavelength lattice cancels the light shift, and its realisation at 1e-18, not the frequency comb and not single-ion control. On timing, the redefinition is a decision by metrology bodies with its own criteria, and the evidence the committee needs is the physics, which is in hand. A prize before the redefinition is therefore not early scientifically. I would only call it early if clock comparisons were still failing to agree, and they do not. I also appreciate that the chair himself moved to B007, since he was the lone first-place vote for B039 and the instrument-builder test is the same one I apply.

uncertainties: Whether the first lattice-clock publications support Katori and Ye alone, or whether Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley or Bloom need to be named. This is checkable and I have not checked it.
Whether colleagues will accept the lattice clock as a discovery of new measurement physics and not an instrument advance, which is a matter of judgement that evidence will not settle.
Whether I am biased in favour of measurement-type results because of my own background.
How much to weigh the unresolved pairing mechanism and the credit gaps in B001 if the experts confirm the credit history and a colleague would move there.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged. I spent a year of my PhD in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall was Jun Ye's mentor at JILA, so I have an indirect link to the group environment of one proposed laureate. I have not collaborated with Ye or Katori, and I see no formal conflict, but I keep the disclosure on record and will recuse if the chair or committee decides it is necessary. My work in Lund atomic physics and quantum memories is adjacent to B008, B015 and B005, none of which is in my preferred configuration.
